title: Tokens

post.author: u/fairbrass_nightmanager_orsolya
post.title: I'm night manager at a travelling carnival. At 23:40 last night our big wheel started after closing, on the sign-in of a man who left on Friday.

blocks.text: I'm Orsolya, night manager of Fairbrass Carnival: 14 rides, 42 staff, a new field weekly. Guests buy a wristband at the gate. It gets you on every ride until it falls off. Nobody phones the gate; they just look at your wrist.

Each ride has a tablet in its control booth, and the operator starts and stops the ride from it. Nikodem, who wrote our ride app, keeps one main computer, holding the staff list, in the office caravan. A computer that answers other machines' requests is called a server.

To use a tablet you sign in once, with your name and password. The server checks both, and that your name is on the staff list. Then it gives the tablet a token: a short note saying who you are and when the note runs out. Ours ran for 30 days.

The server stamps each token with a signature, a mark only the server can make, like a wax seal from a ring nobody else has. On every tap the tablet checks the seal and the date itself, and never asks the server. Nikodem built it that way because our fields often have no signal. Tokens like ours are called JWTs, short for JSON Web Tokens.
Each shared tablet keeps a tile for everyone who has signed in on it, with that person's token saved behind it. At a shift change you tap your tile. No password.

Rupert ran the big wheel. He left us on Friday and handed in his badge and booth key at 18:00. I took him off the staff list that minute: 42 became 41. He never signed out of the wheel's tablet, and nobody cleared his tile.

The wheel ran normally all weekend, and on Tuesday at our new field, from that tablet, under the other operators' tiles. We close at 23:00. At 23:05 the booth was padlocked. Keys: the five wheel operators still with us, the night guard, and me.

At 23:40 the wheel's start horn sounded. From the office caravan I saw the wheel lit and turning, empty. The guard and I reached the booth at 23:51. It had stopped at 23:49. Padlock shut, booth dark, nobody there. Nothing else told anyone: the server never hears a tap.
This morning Nikodem printed these lines from the tablet's ride log. Each line shows the date and time, what was asked, the token's label, whose it is, and the tablet's answer.

22 Sep 16:10  SIGN IN  token 3861  Rupert      issued, good to 22 Oct 16:10
09 Oct 17:25  START    token 3861  Rupert      accepted
09 Oct 17:52  STOP     token 3861  Rupert      accepted
13 Oct 22:58  STOP     token 3907  an operator accepted
13 Oct 23:40  START    token 3861  Rupert      accepted
13 Oct 23:49  STOP     token 3861  Rupert      accepted

blocks.label: big_wheel_tuesday_night.png

diagram.aria: Tuesday night from 22:00 to midnight. The big wheel runs until its last stop at 22:58, is closed and padlocked after that, then runs empty from 23:40:12 to 23:49:30. Token 3861 is valid the whole time. Markers: closing at 23:00, the start at 23:40, and Orsolya and the guard reaching the booth at 23:51.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the ride log and my watch. The wheel's last stop of the night was at 22:58, and the booth was padlocked at 23:05. At 23:40 token 3861 started it, and at 23:49 the same token stopped it, nine minutes of empty cars. Across the whole night token 3861 was valid, as it had been every minute since Friday, and would be until 22 October.

blocks.text: Every line is valid. The seal on token 3861 is real: the server made it on 22 September. It proves who the token was given to, not whose hand is on the tablet. Rupert was at his new job two towns away; his boss confirms it. And nothing can cancel a token before it runs out.
I deleted Rupert's tile at midnight. But every tablet still trusts every token until its date. The wheel opens at 17:00 tonight. What should Nikodem change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A cloakroom ticket and a wristband answer the same question in opposite ways, Orsolya. The cloakroom keeps the record behind its counter, so the counter can tear it up. That's a session, the server's own note of who is signed in. Your seal puts the whole record on the wrist, so a tablet needs nobody, and nobody can take it back. So: how long after Friday 18:00 could Rupert's tile still start the wheel? Did his token ever leave that tablet? And when you took him off the list, which tablet found out?

replies.author: u/fairbrass_nightmanager_orsolya
replies.text: Nikodem says until 22 October at 16:10, nearly 13 days after he left. The token never left that tablet: it sat behind his tile the whole time. And no tablet found out. The list changed on the server, and the tablets never ask it.

comments.author: u/stateless_brigitta
comments.text: Signed tokens are the modern way. The point is that a tablet trusts the seal and never waits on a server, which is exactly why your rides work in a muddy field with no signal. Asking a server on every tap defeats the point. Even renewal, where the tablet swaps a longer-lived ticket at the server for a fresh short token every few minutes, is the server creeping back in. Your problem was one tile nobody cleared, not the design.

comments.author: u/lock_up_feodora
comments.text: Old fairground rule: nothing stays switched on overnight. Sign every tablet out at closing, all tiles gone, and each operator types a password once at the start of a shift. A leaver, anyone who has left the staff, loses their tile that night: Rupert's would have gone at 23:00 on Friday. Cheap, and no new code.

reply.prompt: The wheel opens again at 17:00 tonight, and every tablet still trusts every token until its date. What should Nikodem change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Shorten the tablet sign-in to one hour, so a leaver's token runs out the same evening.
options.verdict: A shorter wait, paid for by everyone
options.part2: Nikodem set every token to run out after one hour, with nothing to renew it. We replayed Friday to Tuesday in the sim. Under that rule Rupert's last sign-in, at 17:25 on Friday, ran out at 18:25, 25 minutes after he left, and Tuesday's 23:40 start was refused. But every operator now types a password every hour: 6 times in a six-hour night, 20 sign-ins in the busiest hour. A token that runs out mid-ride locks the tablet until its operator signs in again; only the red stop button on the booth wall still works. And for those 25 minutes nothing could stop Rupert's token. Someone sent home in the middle of a shift keeps up to an hour.
options.senior: Shortening a token's life shrinks the window but never closes it, and without renewal every hour you cut is paid for by the people using the system. Something still has to be able to say no before the token runs out. Short lifetimes are half the fix; the other half is a regular moment when the server is asked, and can refuse.

options.text: Sign every tablet out at closing time, so no stored token is left for the next night.
options.verdict: Clears the tablet, not the token
options.part2: From Friday the night guard signs every tablet out at 23:00, and each operator types a password at the start of a shift. In the sim, Rupert's tile went at 23:00 on Friday, five hours after he left, and Tuesday's start was refused: signing in again needs a name on the staff list. Feodora is right that it's cheap, and it would have stopped this night. But signing out only deletes the tablet's copy. Token 3861 itself stayed good until 22 October. Someone let go at 14:00 keeps a working tile until 23:00, and a tablet that is switched off at closing, away for repair or out of signal keeps every tile it holds.
options.senior: Clearing shared devices is good practice; keep it. But it removes copies, it cancels nothing: a token stays valid wherever a copy still sits until it runs out. Cancelling has to happen where trust is decided, at the server or in what the tablets check, not on a device you hope holds the only copy.

options.text: Use ten-minute tokens that the server renews only for people still on the staff list.
options.part2: Nikodem changed two things. Each token now lasts ten minutes. Behind every tile the tablet also keeps a refresh token, a longer-lived ticket good for 30 days. When the short token runs out, the tablet shows the ticket to the server, which checks the staff list before it issues a new one. Taps in between are still checked on the tablet alone. We replayed Friday to Tuesday in the sim. Rupert's last short token came at 17:52, with his STOP, and ran out at 18:02, two minutes after I took him off the list. At 23:40 on Tuesday his tile asked for a new one and the server said no: not on the staff list. The wheel never moved. The cost: up to 120 server checks in the busiest hour, against none before, and a tablet out of signal for more than ten minutes has to wait for it; the red stop button works regardless. Nikodem also set the tablets to accept only the one signing method he uses.
options.senior: A signed token is a promise the server can't take back, so keep the promise short and make renewal the moment the server is asked. Short tokens with a refresh token checked against the staff list give a leaver minutes, not weeks, while every tap is still checked on the tablet. Brigitta's worry is fair, but this asks the server once per ten minutes per sign-in, not on every tap. The cost is a server that must be reachable that often, and checks that grow with sign-ins. Pin the signing method too: RFC 8725 asks libraries to let you name the methods you accept.

options.text: Tie each token to the tablet it was issued on, so it can never work on any other tablet.
options.part2: Nikodem tied each token to the tablet it was made on: a tablet now refuses any token made for another. We replayed Friday to Tuesday in the sim. Token 3861 was made on the wheel's tablet on 22 September, and Tuesday's 23:40 start came from that same tablet, so it was accepted and the wheel turned empty again. Rupert's token still worked until 22 October 16:10. Binding stops a token from travelling. This one never travelled.
options.senior: Binding a token to a device helps when tokens might be copied elsewhere; it answers 'is this the right device?', not 'should this person still be allowed in?'. A leaver is a question of cancelling, and binding cancels nothing.

sim.title: Replay Rupert's token from Friday 18:00 to Tuesday 23:59
sim.lede: You're Nikodem, just before 18:00 on Friday, when Rupert hands in his badge and leaves the staff list (42 becomes 41). His tile on the big wheel's tablet holds token 3861, issued on 22 September at 16:10. Choose how long a token lasts (30 days as built; one hour with nothing to renew it; or ten minutes, renewed with a longer-lived ticket good for 30 days), how a token can be cancelled (no way, as built; a deny list, a list of cancelled tokens that tablets download each night at 04:00; or a staff-list check at every renewal), whether every tablet is signed out at 23:00 closing, whether a token is tied to its tablet, and whether tablets accept only the one expected signing method. As given data: Rupert's last sign-in under the one-hour rule would be 17:25 on Friday; under ten-minute tokens his last short token comes with his STOP at 17:52; 20 sign-ins are in use in the busiest hour, and a night is six hours. Then play to Tuesday 23:59. No token is made, changed or read apart here; tokens are labels.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built. Tuesday's 23:40 start is accepted, and the token still works for 12 d 22 h 10 min after Rupert left. Tie tokens to their tablet: nothing changes. Sign tablets out at closing: Tuesday is refused, but the token itself is still good. Try one-hour tokens: refused, 25 min, and 6 password sign-ins a night. Try ten-minute tokens with no check: accepted again, with 120 server checks an hour for nothing. Then add the staff-list check: refused, 2 min.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke a lock. The server sealed token 3861 for Rupert in September and promised it for 30 days, and the tablets keep that promise without asking anyone. Taking him off the staff list changed only the server, which the tablets never consult. Make tokens short and renew them only after the server checks the staff list, and a leaver's token dies within minutes.

steps.title: Two ways to remember who is signed in.
steps.text: A session is the cloakroom way. The server keeps a record of each sign-in and hands out a plain ticket that only points at it. Every request is checked against the record, so the server can end a session at any moment by deleting the record. A signed token is the wristband way. The token carries its own facts, who it was given to and when it runs out, plus a signature. Anyone holding the server's checking key can trust it without asking. That saves a trip to the server on every tap, which is why Nikodem chose it for fields with no signal. The price is that there is no record to delete.

steps.title: What happened, step by step.
steps.text: On 22 September at 16:10 Rupert typed his name and password on the wheel's tablet. The server checked both, and that he was on the staff list. It wrote token 3861: his name, and a run-out time of 22 October 16:10. It added its signature, and the tablet saved the token behind his tile. From then on, every tap on his tile meant three checks on the tablet alone: is the signature good, is the run-out time still ahead, and is the request one an operator may make. On Friday at 18:00 the staff list changed on the server, and no tablet heard. On Tuesday at 23:40 a tap on his tile passed all three checks, exactly as on every day since September.

steps.title: What a signature proves, and what it doesn't.
steps.text: A signature proves that the server made this token and that nobody has changed a letter of it since. It does not prove who is holding it, and it does not prove that anything in it is still true. The token says 'Rupert, operator, good until 22 October'. All of that was true when it was written. The run-out time is the token's only built-in limit; RFC 7519 calls it the exp claim, and once it has passed, the token must be refused.

steps.title: Cancelling a token: short lives, renewal, deny lists.
steps.text: There are three common ways to take a token back before its date. First, keep it short: a ten-minute token can't outlive a leaver by more than ten minutes. Second, renew it with a refresh token, a longer-lived ticket the tablet shows to the server when the short token runs out. The server checks the staff list, and only then writes a new short token, so renewal is the moment the server gets a say. Third, keep a deny list: a list of cancelled tokens that every checker reads. It works only as fast as it reaches the tablets; synced nightly at 04:00, Rupert's token would have died 10 hours after he left. Each way costs server checks: none as built, up to 120 an hour with ten-minute renewal.

steps.title: Check the signing method.
steps.text: Each JWT names the method used to sign it in a field called alg. Some libraries once accepted a token that declared it needed no signature at all, the 'alg: none' family of flaws, because they let the token choose how it would be checked. The defence is simple. The tablet decides the method in advance, from its own settings, and refuses any token that names a different one, or none. RFC 8725 makes this a rule for libraries. It didn't matter last night, because token 3861 was genuinely signed; it closes a different door.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Tuesday 23:40. Rupert's tile, holding token 3861, is tapped on the wheel's tablet. The tablet's ten-minute token has run out, so it asks the server to renew it. The server checks the staff list, which has 41 names and not Rupert's, and a dashed red line back to Rupert's tile is marked refused, 23:40.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Tuesday 23:40. Taps are still checked on the tablet alone, but each token lasts ten minutes. When Rupert's tile is tapped, its short token ran out at 18:02 on Friday, so the tablet asks the server to renew it. The server checks the staff list, finds 41 names and not his, and refuses. The wheel never moves.

fix.title: The fix: ten-minute tokens, renewed only for people still on the staff list
fix.text: Make every token last ten minutes. Behind each tile, keep a refresh token, a longer-lived ticket good for 30 days, which the tablet shows to the server when the short token runs out. Before writing a new short token, the server checks that the person is still on the staff list. Taps between renewals are still checked on the tablet alone, so rides keep working through a few minutes without signal. Set every tablet to accept only the one signing method Nikodem uses, and to refuse tokens that name another or none. Keep Feodora's sign-out at closing as good practice, and keep a small deny list for the rare case where even ten minutes is too long. In the sim, Rupert's last short token runs out at 18:02 on Friday, two minutes after he left, and Tuesday's 23:40 start is refused. The cost is up to 120 server checks in the busiest hour, against none before.

limits: Ten minutes is still ten minutes. For someone removed in anger mid-shift, add the token to a deny list the tablets read at once, or take the tablet; the red stop button doesn't depend on any token.

The refresh token becomes the valuable thing: it lasts 30 days. The server must keep a record of each one so it can cancel them, which is a session by another name, and should refuse renewal after a long idle spell.

Renewal needs the server reachable at least every ten minutes. In a field with no signal, a ride waits until it can renew, so the carnival needs a signal plan, or a longer token and a faster deny list.

explain.seniorTake: Sessions and signed tokens are the same trade seen from two ends. A session keeps the truth on the server, so you can end it at once, and pays with a server trip on every request. A signed token carries its own truth, so anyone can check it alone, and pays with a promise you can't take back. Don't pick a side; pick how long a promise you can live with. Long-lived signed tokens with no way to cancel them are the usual mistake, and the usual victim is the leaver whose access outlasts the job. Short access tokens, renewed with a refresh token only after a server check, give you most of the speed of tokens and most of the control of sessions. Add a small deny list for emergencies and keep it until the tokens on it expire. Then check what a token can't tell you. A signature proves who wrote the token, not who holds it or whether it is still true. Never let the token choose its own signing method.

realWorld.title: RFC 7519: the exp claim
realWorld.text: The JWT standard says the exp claim "identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted for processing", and that "the current date/time MUST be before the expiration date/time listed in the "exp" claim." It allows "some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew." A token's own date is its only built-in limit.

realWorld.title: RFC 8725: the 'alg: none' family
realWorld.text: The JWT best-practice document notes that signed JWTs name their signing algorithm in the alg header, and that "The algorithm can be changed to "none" by an attacker, and some libraries would trust this value and "validate" the JWT without checking any signature." That one sentence is all you need to know about the flaw.

realWorld.title: RFC 8725: perform algorithm verification
realWorld.text: Its section 3.1 is the defence: "Libraries MUST enable the caller to specify a supported set of algorithms and MUST NOT use any other algorithms when performing cryptographic operations." The tablet, not the token, decides the method.

realWorld.title: OWASP: deny lists and short expiry
realWorld.text: OWASP's JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet says "In some cases, the consumer of the token might want to maintain a JWT denylist", and "A JWT deny list can typically be implemented based on the jti and iss claims" (the token's id and who issued it). Before building one, it lists better options, including: "Token reuse can be mitigated by using short expiration time in the JWT."

realWorld.title: OWASP: refuse 'none'
realWorld.text: The same cheat sheet says "Some JWT libraries, used to accept unsecured JWTs by default", and its mitigation is plain: "Make sure that "alg":"none" is not accepted by your JWT parser."

realWorld.title: RFC 6749: what a refresh token is
realWorld.text: The OAuth 2.0 standard says "Refresh tokens are credentials used to obtain access tokens", used "to obtain a new access token when the current access token becomes invalid or expires", and notes that access tokens "may have a shorter lifetime". The renewal step is where the server gets its say.

asked: Sessions or JWTs: what does each cost you?
How do you revoke a JWT?
What is a refresh token for?
interview.answer: A session keeps the record on the server and gives the client a plain id. Every request looks it up, so you can end a session at once by deleting it; the cost is a lookup on every request and a store every server can reach. A JWT carries its own claims and a signature, so any service holding the key can check it alone, with no lookup; the cost is that once issued it is valid until its exp time, and nothing in the token can take that back. So 'how do you revoke a JWT' really means 'where do you put a check'. The usual answer is short-lived access tokens, a few minutes, plus a refresh token that the client trades for a new access token. The server checks, at every renewal, that the user still exists, still has the role, and that the refresh token itself hasn't been cancelled. That bounds a leaver to one access-token lifetime. For emergencies, add a deny list of token ids that checkers read, kept until those tokens expire, and accept that it is only as fast as it spreads. Store refresh tokens on the server side so you can cancel them per device. And validate properly: pin the expected algorithm rather than trusting the alg header (RFC 8725 section 3.1; the 'alg: none' flaws came from libraries that trusted it), check exp, the issuer (who made it) and the audience (who it is for). A story I'd tell: a carnival gave ride tablets 30-day signed tokens checked offline. An operator left on a Friday and his saved token started the big wheel after closing on Tuesday, because taking him off the staff list reached nothing that checked. Ten-minute tokens renewed only after a staff-list check would have refused it, two minutes after he left.

terms.def: The travelling carnival in this story: 14 rides, 42 staff, and a new field most weeks.
The person in charge of a carnival after closing. Orsolya is Fairbrass Carnival's.
A band a guest buys at the gate that gets them on every ride until it falls off. Ride staff look at it; they never phone the gate.
The tablet in each ride's control booth that operators use to start and stop the ride.
A computer that answers other machines' requests. Fairbrass Carnival's sits in the office caravan and holds the staff list.
The server's list of everyone who works at the carnival: 42 names on Friday before 18:00, 41 after.
A short note the server gives a device after sign-in, saying who you are and when the note runs out. Like a wristband.
A mark on a token that only the server can make, like a wax seal. It proves the server made the token and nobody changed it; not who holds it.
A token that carries its own facts and a signature, so any device can check it without asking the server.
Short for JSON Web Token: a common format for signed tokens. Fairbrass Carnival's tablets use JWTs.
A button on a shared tablet for each person who has signed in on it, with that person's token saved behind it. Tapping it needs no password.
Rupert's token on the big wheel's tablet, issued on 22 September at 16:10 and good for 30 days, until 22 October at 16:10.
The tablet's record of every request: date, time, action, token label, whose it is, and whether the tablet accepted it.
The horn a big wheel sounds before it starts to move. It is what told Orsolya at 23:40.
Someone who has left the company. Their access should end when they do.
The server's own record of who is signed in, like a cloakroom's record behind the counter. The server can end it at once by deleting the record.
The moment a token runs out and must be refused. In a JWT it is the exp claim.
The field in a JWT that holds its expiry time. RFC 7519 says the token must not be accepted on or after it.
One fact written inside a token, such as who it is for or when it runs out.
How long a token lasts from when it is issued: 30 days, one hour or ten minutes in this case.
Swapping a longer-lived ticket at the server for a fresh short token when the old one runs out. The server can refuse.
The longer-lived ticket used for renewal. The tablet shows it to the server, which checks the staff list before writing a new short token.
The short-lived token that is checked on every tap, as opposed to the refresh token used to get a new one.
Cancelling a token before its expiry. A plain signed token has no built-in way to do it.
A list of cancelled tokens that every checker reads and refuses. It works only as fast as it reaches them.
Deleting the saved token from a device. It removes that copy; it does not cancel the token.
Tying a token to the device it was issued on, so another device refuses it. It stops a token travelling, not a leaver.
The recipe used to make and check a signature. A JWT names it in a field called alg. Also called the signing algorithm.
A family of flaws: some JWT libraries once accepted a token that declared it needed no signature. The defence is to accept only the expected method.
Ready-made code a program uses for a common job, such as checking JWTs.
A working phone or network connection. Many of the carnival's fields have none, which is why the tablets check tokens alone.
Short for Request for Comments: the numbered documents that define internet standards.
The standard that defines JWTs, including the exp claim.
JSON Web Token Best Current Practices: how to use JWTs safely, including checking the signing algorithm.
The OAuth 2.0 standard, which defines refresh tokens.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes free guidance on web application security, including a JSON Web Token cheat sheet.
An international standard for managing information security. Its Annex A lists controls, including removing access rights and secure authentication.
An audit of a company's security controls against the Trust Services Criteria. CC6.2 and CC6.3 cover giving and removing access.
A hands-on project night in the course where you build what several cases taught.

atWork: Look for any token your systems issue that lives longer than a working day, and ask what happens when the person it belongs to leaves this afternoon. It is a common pattern: a mobile app or an internal tool gets long-lived signed tokens 'so people don't have to sign in again', and nobody notices until a leaver's access outlasts the job by days or weeks. For each kind of token, write down its lifetime, what checks it (and whether that checker ever asks a server), how you would cancel one today, and how long that would take to reach every checker. Check your shared devices too: tills, kiosks, warehouse scanners and ride tablets that keep several people signed in. Then shorten access tokens, renew them only after a server check of the person's status, keep a deny list for emergencies, and pin the signing algorithm in your library settings. In Build Night N5 you build roles, hashed API keys, tenant isolation and an audit log into one service; make leaving part of the test: remove a user and prove their next request is refused. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, this is Annex A 5.18 (access rights, removed on leaving) and 8.5 (secure authentication); if it is pursuing SOC 2, it is CC6.2 (credentials removed when access is no longer authorized) and CC6.3 (access removed based on roles and changes). A token that outlives a leaver's removal is a finding an auditor is likely to raise under each, so set token lifetimes and a tested removal path from the first draft rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's staff app issues signed tokens valid for 7 days, and each internal service checks them on its own without asking any server. On Monday an employee is let go and removed from the HR system. On Wednesday her saved token still opens the admin pages. A colleague says to cut tokens to one hour and leave it there. What went wrong, and what would you build?

keyIdeas.idea: A signed token stays valid until it expires; the services never ask, so removing her changed nothing they check
Use short access tokens renewed with a refresh token, and check the person's status at every renewal
Keep a deny list of cancelled tokens for urgent cases, read by every checker until those tokens expire

recall.model: A signed token is valid until it expires, and the services check it alone and never ask anyone, so removing her from HR changed nothing they check: there was no way to cancel it. One-hour tokens on their own only shrink that window and make everyone sign in every hour. Instead, issue short access tokens of a few minutes and a refresh token; at every renewal the server checks she is still employed and that the refresh token hasn't been cancelled, so a leaver is cut off within one access-token lifetime. For urgent cases keep a deny list of cancelled token ids that every service reads, kept until those tokens expire. And pin the signing algorithm in the library settings.

recall.prompt: What does the signature on token 3861 prove?
options: That the person tapping the tile is Rupert
That the server made the token and nobody has changed it since
That Rupert is still on the staff list
That the token has never been used on another tablet
recall.why: A signature proves who wrote the token and that it is unchanged. It says nothing about who holds it, or whether what it says is still true; Rupert had left the staff list four days before.

recall.prompt: In the sim, which setting refuses Tuesday's 23:40 start and leaves Rupert's token working for at most ten minutes after he left?
options: One-hour tokens with nothing to renew them
Ten-minute tokens, renewed only after a staff-list check
Ten-minute tokens, swapped for new ones with no check
recall.why: His last short token ran out at 18:02, two minutes after he left, and the server refused to renew it. One-hour tokens also refuse Tuesday but leave 25 minutes; renewal with no check keeps him going until 22 October; binding changes nothing.

recall.prompt: What is the 'alg: none' family of JWT flaws, and what is the defence?
options: Tokens with no expiry; the defence is a nightly sync
Some libraries once accepted a token that declared it needed no signature; accept only the expected signing method
Tokens signed with a weak password; the defence is a slow hash
Tokens sent in page addresses; the defence is to send them in a header
recall.why: The flaw came from letting the token choose how it is checked. RFC 8725 says libraries must let the caller name the supported algorithms and must not use any other.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Ten-minute tokens, renewal checked against the staff list, and not one leaver's tile has worked past ten minutes since. In March, on the road between two fields, the ghost train's tablet fell off a lorry and was never found. Seven people had tiles on it, all still on the staff, each with a refresh token good for 30 days. Nikodem's server log shows that tablet renewing one of those tiles at 02:10 three nights later, and the server saying yes: the name was still on the staff list.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the server renew a tile on a lost tablet, and what should Nikodem build so a lost device can be cut off?

keyIdeas.idea: The renewal check asks only whether the person is still staff; they are, so the refresh token still works
The server should keep a record of every refresh token per device, so all of a lost tablet's tickets can be cancelled at once
Limit refresh tokens: a shorter life, refusal after an idle spell, or a fresh password after a gap

coldCase.model: The renewal check only asks whether the person is still staff, and all seven still are, so a refresh token on a lost tablet keeps working for up to 30 days. Nothing checks the device. Have the server keep a record of each refresh token per device, so Nikodem can cancel every ticket the lost tablet holds in one go, and the next renewal from it is refused. That record is a small session store, and that's the point: the long-lived ticket is the one you must be able to cancel. Also limit refresh tokens: refuse renewal after an idle spell of a few hours, so a tablet unused overnight needs a fresh password, and ask the seven people to sign in again on a new tablet.
